keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Whether this is for the user themselves, a family member, or someone else changes the angle of research — eligibility requirements, age limits, and application framing all shift.
Apprenticeship programs are almost always location-specific — unions, trade schools, and employers vary drastically by region, so geography narrows the search immediately.
Carpentry has sub-specialties (rough framing, finish carpentry, cabinetry, formwork) — knowing the target specialty focuses which programs are actually relevant.
Some programs require full-time commitment; others are part-time. Existing work, school, or family obligations could rule out certain formats entirely.
Union vs. non-union apprenticeships differ in wages, benefits, job placement, and culture — a strong preference here eliminates a large category of programs.
The user may be optimizing for fastest completion, highest pay, best employer reputation, or a specific credential — this determines how programs should be ranked and evaluated.
Knowing whether the user wants a compiled list, a comparison table, direct application links, or just a starting point determines the format and depth of the research output.

gold.taskDescription: Find and evaluate carpentry apprenticeship programs that match the user's situation, goals, and constraints.

questions.title: Who is this apprenticeship research for?
questions.description: Determine whether the research is for the user personally, a child or family member, or someone else — this affects eligibility filtering and how the information should be framed.

questions.title: What city, state, or country should programs be in?
questions.description: Pin down the geographic area so the research targets locally available programs, unions, and trade schools rather than irrelevant national or international options.

questions.title: Is there a specific type of carpentry to focus on?
questions.description: Identify whether the focus is rough framing, finish carpentry, cabinetry, formwork, or general carpentry so only relevant program tracks are included.

questions.title: Are there scheduling or time availability constraints?
questions.description: Establish whether full-time, part-time, or evening-only programs are needed based on existing work, school, or personal commitments.

questions.title: Is there a preference for union or non-union programs?
questions.description: Determine whether union-affiliated programs (e.g., UBC/JATC) or non-union/employer-sponsored apprenticeships are preferred, since this filters a large portion of available options.

questions.title: What matters most when comparing programs — pay, speed, or credentials?
questions.description: Identify the top priority — highest starting wage, shortest path to journeyman status, or a specific certification — so programs can be ranked meaningfully.

questions.title: What should the final research output look like?
questions.description: Clarify whether the user wants a simple list of programs, a side-by-side comparison, direct application links, or a step-by-step action plan for applying.
